Alex has been getting into frequent fights and displaying verbal aggression toward other students and school staff. Alex's mentor， who genuinely cares about him， asked how he was feeling.
Alex， who likes and trusts his mentor， confided that he has been going through a difficult time at home. His parents are now divorced because his mother has found a new partner.

Anyone Can Report Concerns':Anyone， including children and teenagers， can contact social services if they are worried about someone who is struggling and not receiving help， such as when parents are unable to care for them due to illness， conflict， or substance use; when someone engages in self-harm， skips school， fights， or participates in illegal activities; when someone faces overly strict rules， relationship restrictions， or family threats; or when someone has been a victim of a crime and needs counseling， information， or support.

A few days ago， Alex returned home as usual. His father， still overwhelmed by sadness from the breakup and his ex-wife's departure， remained deeply consumed by his emotions. This has been the situation for a while.
Hey， Dad.
(Watching TV) You're back， Alex. Grab me a couple of beers from the fridge， will you?
(Brings the beer) Dad， you should drink less. You've been drinking too much lately.
How was your day? Was today alright?
Not really. The test results came out， and my grades weren't great. And I also had some... issues with John. I told you about him before.
Oh， I see...
Alex.
Yes， dad?
Alex.
I'm here， Dad.
Oh， my Alex. Look at you. You've grown so much.
I don't know how to keep going， Alex. I feel like I can't take it anymore.
... Everything will be okay， Dad.
I loved her so much. How could she just leave me like that?
I remember that trip to Norway with her， before you were even born. We were so happy back then.
She always had that bright smile on her face. She insisted on feeding the seagulls with our bread — they nearly stole our lunch.
Ungrateful little creatures， haha. We laughed so much that day. I loved her so much. Why? I loved her so much.
Dad...
Why， Alex? Why did she leave me? How could she just walk away from us like that? Why， Alex? She has no idea how much pain I'm in.
She doesn't get it! She doesn't care!
Alex， your mother is a heartless woman， do you hear me? She doesn't care at all! She doesn't care!
Dad， I should go do my homework...
Forget your homework， Alex! It's worthless， just like that heartless woman! Worthless! Marriage vows， promises — all lies! Just empty words!
I'm so hurt， Alex. I'm so， so hurt.

I contacted Alex's teacher， and the teacher expressed understanding of Alex's difficult situation. His father is consumed by his sadness， frequently expressing to Alex how heartbroken he feels， while his mother is deeply involved in her new relationship.

Alex feels insignificant and unnoticed， and he is also very worried about his father. After learning about the teacher's concerns， I first assessed whether Alex needed immediate social services assistance. I concluded that Alex was not currently at risk of harm. The next step was to...
Invite Alex’s family to a meeting
Invite the teacher and Alex’s family to a meeting
Since Alex has great trust in his teacher and feels safer with his presence， he requested to have his teacher attend the meeting.

‘Signs of Safety’: One of the core approaches used by social workers is the Signs of Safety method. This approach emphasizes involving the child (depending on their age and maturity)， parents， and other trusted individuals throughout the investigation， social interventions， and follow-ups. These individuals may include relatives， teachers， neighbors， older siblings， or a friend’s parents — essentially anyone the family trusts and who can provide a positive influence. By applying this principle， we aim to help the child feel safer and more comfortable.

I invited the parents， Alex， and his teacher to the meeting. During the meeting， the teacher and I explained why we were concerned about Alex. After listening to Alex， his parents， and his teacher， I concluded that Alex’s parents were not providing the necessary care for him. Therefore， I initiated an investigation.
During the investigation， what do you think Alex’s biggest problem is:
Lack of financial support from his parents
Lack of emotional support from his parents
Being too immature and not independent enough
You think Alex’s father is too poor， which caused Alex’s mother to leave them and prevented his father from rebuilding his life.
Of course， you keep this thought to yourself because you know bringing it up won’t lead to a good outcome.

You believe the main issue is that Alex’s father is consumed by his sorrow， and his mother is solely focused on her new relationship， leaving Alex without adequate emotional support. As parents， they have not fulfilled this essential responsibility.

You are right. When you brought up this point during the family meeting， the parents fell silent. You recommended a family therapist to help them learn how to become better parents and take responsibility for their child’s well-being.
During the family meeting， you claim that Alex’s biggest problem is his lack of independence and self-control. Alex says， 'But I’m only nine!' Alex’s teacher exclaims， 'Oh my god.'

Clearly， Alex’s biggest issue is the lack of emotional support from his parents. Apart from his teacher， there is no one providing him with the emotional care he needs. Unfortunately， the teacher's support has its limits， so it is now up to Alex’s parents to step up and make a real effort.

We created a plan to gather a clearer picture of the family's situation. Together， we listed people familiar with the family， including school staff， relatives， and others who know them well. I explained to Alex and his parents that I would contact these individuals to collect more information.

Later， we identified two people within Alex’s family network who could offer meaningful support: Alex’s uncle and his grandmother. Now， back to the problem. Alex’s father’s constant venting to Alex every day has clearly become a major factor affecting him. How do you think this issue should be addressed?
Tell Alex’s father， 'Grow up!'
Suggest that Alex’s father talk to Alex’s uncle instead when he needs to vent.
Try to encourage Alex’s mother to reconcile with Alex’s father.

You tell Alex’s father， 'You really should grow up! Take responsibility!'Alex’s father is shocked， looks up at you in surprise， and doesn’t say anything. It seems that reprimanding this man， who is suffering emotionally， doesn’t help solve the problem.

You discuss the issue with Alex’s uncle， who reports that Alex’s father has been upset and struggling to cope since the separation. Both the grandmother and uncle believe that Alex’s parents are currently unable to meet his needs or fulfill their roles as adults.
You talk to Alex’s father about the situation， and he agrees to call his brother when he feels the need to talk about his emotions， instead of talking to Alex.

You repeatedly try to subtly push Alex’s parents to reconcile during the family meetings， which clearly turns out to be a foolish approach. Your efforts are met with resistance from both sides， and your excessive involvement in their personal lives is criticized by your supervisor. Your colleagues even start calling you 'Cupid，' and they refer to this case as 'Cupid’s Boomerang Plan.'
So， for Alex's emotional issues at school， the solution you propose is:
Tell Alex， 'Grow up!'
Have Alex’s teacher be stricter with him.
Have Alex’s grandmother care for him from time to time
'But I’m only nine!”'Alex shouted. It seems that telling Alex to 'grow up' is not an appropriate response given his age and the emotional strain he’s facing.

I believe what Alex needs right now isn’t more behavioral control. What he really needs is emotional support，' Alex’s teacher said. The teacher’s perspective suggests that the key issue is not about disciplining Alex more but offering the emotional care and support he is lacking.

When you suggested that Alex’s grandmother might provide emotional support， she expressed her willingness to help. She really cares for her grandson， and although she had suggested this before， Alex’s father had always opposed it.

Alex’s father is reluctant to let his child be away from him. After further discussions， the family came to a consensus: on weekends， Alex will spend time with his grandparents， giving him a different environment and the emotional support he needs.

After careful assessment， you reached an important conclusion: Alex's parents need to better understand how their behaviors are affecting their child and be clear about the steps they need to take to meet Alex’s needs. They also need to learn to cooperate and work together to address issues concerning Alex.

To help them achieve these goals， you suggested family therapy. Through patient communication， both parents agreed to this plan. Meanwhile， to meet Alex's need for emotional support from trusted adults， the family decided that next month， Alex would spend weekends with his grandmother to receive additional care. Alex's father decided that when he needs to talk about his emotions， he would call his brother instead of venting directly to Alex.

I promised to closely monitor the situation of Alex， his parents， grandmother， and uncle to ensure that these changes would genuinely improve the family dynamics. Over the following weeks， I made several phone calls to each family member to understand their feelings and family dynamics. I also proactively contacted the parents' family therapist to gather professional feedback.

Fortunately， everyone felt that things were improving. Alex became happier and his emotions were no longer as easily triggered. The family therapist reported that the parents had gradually recognized the impact of their behavior on Alex and were actively working on future action plans.

Alex's mother and he spent at least two weekdays together every week， and they also spent time together every other weekend. His father focused on moving forward from the difficulties of separation while receiving emotional support from his brother.

As family relationships improved， everyone agreed that they no longer required further intervention from the social services department. I was pleased to close the case， wishing the family continued positive changes in the future.

After a conflict with the restaurant supervisor， she stopped going to the restaurant. Her parents later reported that she was hanging out with gang members again. I tried to contact Kim and persuade her to try a new approach， but she refused. The case ended.
A month later， you received a call， and the voice of a young boy came through the phone.
Hi， who is speaking?
Hi， it's Alex.
Hey there， little Alex， how have you been?
I'm doing great! I'm at my grandmother's house now. I don't fight at school anymore， am i a good boy？
Really? That's awesome， Alex! You're such a good kid.
Hehe， if it's okay， I’d like to stay in touch with you.
Of course， feel free to contact me anytime if you need anything!
That's great， then it’s settled. Bye-bye!
Bye!
